title: Run a linear Kalman predict/update and fusion check
scope: Predict/update of a declared scalar or 2-state constant-velocity linear-Gaussian model with one scalar measurement: innovation, gain, posterior covariance, sequential versus information-form fusion, a correlated-noise counterexample and NIS on a replay; no EKF/UKF, tuning, ensemble statistics or hardware

routeNotes.scalar-fusion: One scalar state: a single update, two independent sensors fused in sequence and checked against the batch information form, then a correlated-noise counterexample where the independence assumption fails.
routeNotes.constant-velocity: A position-velocity state: prediction with F and Q, a position-only update with a cross-covariance correction, and a replay with a dropout, NIS and the false-failure rate of a chi-square gate.

items.prompt: A kiln controller tracks the wall temperature T (°C) as a scalar Kalman state. After its prediction step the declared prior is T = 20 °C with variance P = 2.5 °C². A thermocouple measures the state directly, z = H T + v with H = 1 and independent noise of declared variance R = 1.5 °C², and reads z = 23 °C. Assume the prior, H and R are exactly right. Compute the innovation y = z - H T (°C), its variance S = H P H + R (°C²), the Kalman gain K (dimensionless here), and the posterior mean (°C) and variance (°C²). Each answer is graded within ±0.001.
items.solution: Innovation y = z - H x = 23 - 20 = 3 °C. Innovation variance S = H P H + R = 2.5 + 1.5 = 4 °C². Gain K = P H / S = 2.5/4 = 0.625. Posterior mean x = 20 + 0.625·3 = 21.875 °C. Posterior variance P = (1 - K H) P = 0.375·2.5 = 0.9375 °C², below both the prior 2.5 and the sensor 1.5. Check with the information form: 1/P = 1/2.5 + 1/1.5 = 1.066667, so P = 0.9375, and x = P·(20/2.5 + 23/1.5) = 21.875.
hints: Work in the order the filter does: first the innovation y and its variance S, then the gain from the prior variance and S, and only then the posterior mean and variance.
S adds the prior variance (through H) and the sensor variance R; K is the prior variance times H divided by that S. Then x = prior mean + K y and P = (1 - K H) times the prior variance.

Innovation y = z - H x = 23 - 20 = 3 °C. Innovation variance S = H P H + R = 2.5 + 1.5 = 4 °C². Gain K = P H / S = 2.5/4 = 0.625. Posterior mean x = 20 + 0.625·3 = 21.875 °C. Posterior variance P = (1 - K H) P = 0.375·2.5 = 0.9375 °C², below both the prior 2.5 and the sensor 1.5. Check with the information form: 1/P = 1/2.5 + 1/1.5 = 1.066667, so P = 0.9375, and x = P·(20/2.5 + 23/1.5) = 21.875.
items.remediation: Common slips on this item: leaving the prior variance out of S (K = P/R = 1.666667) pushes the mean to 25 °C; flipping the innovation (x - z) moves the mean the wrong way, to 18.125 °C; keeping the prior variance 2.5 °C² after the update forgets that a measurement reduces uncertainty. Re-derive S, K and P step by step, then try a fresh X27 item.

items.prompt: A water tank level L (litres) is the scalar state, with declared prior mean 50 L and variance 9 L². At the same instant two independent sensors measure the level directly (H = 1 for both): a float gauge reads 54 L with noise variance 3 L², and a pressure sensor reads 51 L with noise variance 6 L². Apply the Kalman update for the float gauge, then for the pressure sensor on the result, with no prediction between them. Report the mean (L) and variance (L²) after the float gauge alone, and after both. Then check against the batch information form: report the posterior precision Y = 1/P0 + 1/R1 + 1/R2 in L⁻². Each answer is graded within ±0.001.
items.solution: After sensor A: S = 9 + 3 = 12, K = 9/12 = 0.75, mean = 50 + 0.75·(54 - 50) = 53 L, variance = (1 - 0.75)·9 = 2.25 L². After sensor B (prior is now 53 L, 2.25 L²): S = 2.25 + 6 = 8.25, K = 2.25/8.25 = 0.272727, mean = 53 + 0.272727·(51 - 53) = 52.454545 L, variance = (1 - 0.272727)·2.25 = 1.636364 L². Batch information form: Y = 1/9 + 1/3 + 1/6 = 0.611111 L⁻², so P = 1/Y = 1.636364 L² and mean = P·(50/9 + 54/3 + 51/6) = 52.454545 L: precisions add, and the same posterior comes out whichever sensor is processed first.
hints: Each sequential update uses the previous posterior as its prior, both mean AND variance. The information form is the check: inverse variances (precisions) simply add.
First update: S = P0 + R1, K = P0/S, mean = prior + K (z1 - prior), variance = (1 - K) P0. Repeat with those results as the new prior and the pressure sensor. For Y, add 1/9, 1/3 and 1/6.

After sensor A: S = 9 + 3 = 12, K = 9/12 = 0.75, mean = 50 + 0.75·(54 - 50) = 53 L, variance = (1 - 0.75)·9 = 2.25 L². After sensor B (prior is now 53 L, 2.25 L²): S = 2.25 + 6 = 8.25, K = 2.25/8.25 = 0.272727, mean = 53 + 0.272727·(51 - 53) = 52.454545 L, variance = (1 - 0.272727)·2.25 = 1.636364 L². Batch information form: Y = 1/9 + 1/3 + 1/6 = 0.611111 L⁻², so P = 1/Y = 1.636364 L² and mean = P·(50/9 + 54/3 + 51/6) = 52.454545 L: precisions add, and the same posterior comes out whichever sensor is processed first.
items.remediation: Common slips on this item: reusing the original variance 9 for the second update gives a final mean of 51.8 L instead of the carried-forward one; averaging prior and both readings equally gives 51.666667 L and ignores the declared variances; adding variances for the batch check (9 + 3 + 6 = 18) instead of adding precisions. Carry both mean and variance forward, then try a fresh X27 item.

items.prompt: Two range sensors measure the same distance d (m) with no usable prior (treat the prior variance as infinite, so only the sensors count). Their declared noise variances are R1 = 1 m² and R2 = 4 m², and each declared variance equals that sensor's true noise variance, but both share a power supply, so their noise errors are actually correlated with coefficient ρ = 0.6 (Cov = ρ √(R1 R2)). The filter ignores this and fuses them as independent with the information form, which fixes the weights w_i proportional to 1/R_i. Report the variance the filter claims (m²), the true error variance of that same weighted estimate under the correlated noise (m², graded within ±0.001), and choose how the claimed variance compares with the true one.

fields.label: True error variance of the fused value (m²)
The claimed variance is
fields.answer: Too small: the filter is overconfident about the fused value
options: Too large: the filter is underconfident about the fused value
Too small: the filter is overconfident about the fused value
Too small, but only because R1 and R2 were set too low
Too large, but only because R1 and R2 were set too high

items.solution: Treating the sensors as independent gives claimed precision 1/1 + 1/4 = 1.25, so claimed variance = 0.8 m² and weights w1 = 0.8, w2 = 0.2. The weights are fixed numbers, so the true error of the fused value is w1 e1 + w2 e2 and its variance is w1² r1 + w2² r2 + 2 ρ w1 w2 √(r1 r2) = 0.64 + 0.16 + 2·0.6·0.8·0.2·2 = 1.184 m², which is 1.48 times the claimed value. A positive correlation makes the claimed variance too small: the filter is overconfident and a later NIS test would flag it. The declared variances were right, so retuning R1 or R2 cannot fix this; the independence assumption was not. A fresh run with newly drawn noise will show the same mismatch, because it is built into the model, not into one sample.
hints: The fused value is a fixed weighted sum of the two readings, so its true error variance follows from the covariance matrix of the two noises, whatever the filter believes. First get the weights from the claimed (independent) information form.
Claimed variance = 1/(1/R1 + 1/R2) with weights w_i = (1/R_i) times that. True variance = w1² R1 + w2² R2 + 2 ρ w1 w2 √(R1 R2); compare the two numbers to pick the option.

Treating the sensors as independent gives claimed precision 1/1 + 1/4 = 1.25, so claimed variance = 0.8 m² and weights w1 = 0.8, w2 = 0.2. The declared variances were right, so retuning R1 or R2 cannot fix this; the independence assumption was not. items.remediation: Common slips on this item: reporting the claimed 0.8 m² as the true value ignores the cross term; subtracting the cross term gives 0.416 m² and wrongly suggests the filter is underconfident; using ρ itself instead of the covariance ρ√(R1 R2) shrinks the cross term. Correlation is an assumption violation, not a tuning error, so retuning R would not remove it. Try a fresh X27 item.

items.prompt: A cart on a rail is tracked with a constant-velocity Kalman model, state x = (position in m, velocity in m/s). The current estimate is position 2 m, velocity 1.5 m/s, with covariance P = diag(0.5 m², 0.2 m²/s²) (no cross term). Predict forward by dt = 0.5 s with F = [[1, dt], [0, 1]] and process noise Q = q·[[dt³/3, dt²/2], [dt²/2, dt]] with q = 1.2 m²/s³. Report the predicted position (m) and velocity (m/s) and the predicted covariance entries P00, P01 and P11 (P is symmetric). Each answer is graded within ±0.001.
items.solution: Constant-velocity model: F = [[1, dt], [0, 1]] = [[1, 0.5], [0, 1]], and Q = q·[[dt³/3, dt²/2], [dt²/2, dt]] = 1.2·[[0.041667, 0.125], [0.125, 0.5]] = [[0.05, 0.15], [0.15, 0.6]]. Mean: position = 2 + 0.5·1.5 = 2.75 m, velocity = 1.5 m/s. Covariance P⁻ = F P Fᵀ + Q with P = diag(0.5, 0.2): P00 = 0.5 + 0.5²·0.2 + 0.05 = 0.6, P01 = 0.5·0.2 + 0.15 = 0.25, P11 = 0.2 + 0.6 = 0.8. The position variance grows because velocity uncertainty leaks into position over the step, and the cross-covariance P01 appears even though P started diagonal.
hints: Build F and Q from dt and q first, then propagate the mean with F and the covariance with F P Fᵀ + Q. The covariance transpose goes on the right factor.
Q = [[0.05, 0.15], [0.15, 0.6]] here. F P Fᵀ for a diagonal P has P00 + dt² P11 in the top-left and dt P11 off the diagonal; add Q entry by entry.

Constant-velocity model: F = [[1, dt], [0, 1]] = [[1, 0.5], [0, 1]], and Q = q·[[dt³/3, dt²/2], [dt²/2, dt]] = 1.2·[[0.041667, 0.125], [0.125, 0.5]] = [[0.05, 0.15], [0.15, 0.6]]. Mean: position = 2 + 0.5·1.5 = 2.75 m, velocity = 1.5 m/s. Covariance P⁻ = F P Fᵀ + Q with P = diag(0.5, 0.2): P00 = 0.5 + 0.5²·0.2 + 0.05 = 0.6, P01 = 0.5·0.2 + 0.15 = 0.25, P11 = 0.2 + 0.6 = 0.8. The position variance grows because velocity uncertainty leaks into position over the step, and the cross-covariance P01 appears even though P started diagonal.
items.remediation: Common slips on this item: using Fᵀ P F instead of F P Fᵀ gives P00 = 0.55, P01 = 0.4, P11 = 0.925; leaving Q out gives P00 = 0.55, P01 = 0.1, P11 = 0.2. Check that P01 is nonzero after a step, then try a fresh X27 item.

items.prompt: A rail cart's predicted state is position 4.2 m, velocity 0.8 m/s with covariance P = [[0.9, 0.3], [0.3, 0.5]] (units m², m²/s, m²/s²). A laser measures position only: z = H x + v with H = [1, 0] and declared noise variance R = 0.6 m², and reads z = 4.8 m. Compute the innovation variance S (m²), the gain components K_pos and K_vel, the posterior position (m) and velocity (m/s), and the posterior velocity variance P11 (m²/s²). Assume the model and noise are exactly as declared. Each answer is graded within ±0.001.
items.solution: Position-only measurement, H = [1, 0]. Innovation y = 4.8 - 4.2 = 0.6 m. P Hᵀ is the first column of P = (0.9, 0.3), so S = 0.9 + 0.6 = 1.5 m² and K = (0.9, 0.3)/1.5 = (0.6, 0.2). Posterior mean: position = 4.2 + 0.6·0.6 = 4.56 m, velocity = 0.8 + 0.2·0.6 = 0.92 m/s: the velocity is corrected through the cross-covariance 0.3 although only position was measured. Posterior covariance (I - K H) P: P00 = 0.9 - 0.6·0.9 = 0.36, P11 = 0.5 - 0.2·0.3 = 0.44 m²/s², below the prior 0.5. Check: the information form gives the same P11.
hints: With H = [1, 0], H x is just the position and P Hᵀ is the first column of P. Get S, then K = P Hᵀ / S, a two-component gain.
Both state components move by K times the same innovation y. Then P_post = (I - K H) P, or P minus K S Kᵀ; the velocity variance is the second diagonal entry.

Position-only measurement, H = [1, 0]. Innovation y = 4.8 - 4.2 = 0.6 m. P Hᵀ is the first column of P = (0.9, 0.3), so S = 0.9 + 0.6 = 1.5 m² and K = (0.9, 0.3)/1.5 = (0.6, 0.2). Posterior mean: position = 4.2 + 0.6·0.6 = 4.56 m, velocity = 0.8 + 0.2·0.6 = 0.92 m/s: the velocity is corrected through the cross-covariance 0.3 although only position was measured. Posterior covariance (I - K H) P: P00 = 0.9 - 0.6·0.9 = 0.36, P11 = 0.5 - 0.2·0.3 = 0.44 m²/s², below the prior 0.5. Check: the information form gives the same P11.
items.remediation: Common slips on this item: dividing by R alone (K = P Hᵀ/R) gives a position of 5.1 m and a velocity of 1.1 m/s; ignoring the velocity correction (velocity stays 0.8 m/s) forgets the cross-covariance; leaving the velocity variance at the prior 0.5 m²/s² forgets it is reduced through P01. Recompute S first, then try a fresh X27 item.

items.prompt: Replay a logged laser track for a rail cart with the constant-velocity model, state (position in m, velocity in m/s). Start: position 0 m, velocity 2 m/s, P = diag(1 m², 0.5 m²/s²). Each step is dt = 1 s: F = [[1, dt], [0, 1]], Q = q·[[dt³/3, dt²/2], [dt²/2, dt]] with q = 0.3 m²/s³. The laser measures position only (H = [1, 0], R = 0.4 m²). Per step: predict, then update only if a reading exists. The log is z = 2.3 m at step 1, no reading (dropout) at step 2, z = 10.6 m at step 3. After step 3 report the position (m), velocity (m/s), position variance P00 (m²) and the step-3 NIS = y²/S (computed from the step-3 innovation before its update). Each is graded within ±0.001. Then choose: if the declared model and noise were exactly true, about what fraction of steps would have NIS above a gate of 6.635 (chi-square distribution with 1 degree of freedom)?

fields.label: Fraction of steps above the gate under a correct model

items.solution: Step 1 (z = 2.3): predict to (2, 2) with P⁻ = F P Fᵀ + Q; update with the laser. Step 2 is a dropout: predict only, so the position variance grows and no NIS exists. Step 3 (z = 10.6): predict again to position 6.435 m, velocity 2.0975 m/s, innovation y = 4.165 m with S = 4.395 m², so NIS = y²/S = 3.947036. After the update the state is position 10.220933 m, velocity 3.905176 m/s, P00 = 0.363595 m². The gate 6.635 is the 99th percentile of chi-square with 1 degree of freedom (y/sqrt(S) beyond about 2.58 standard deviations), so if the declared model and R were exactly true only about 1% of steps would exceed it by chance. A single exceedance would therefore not be proof of a fault, and this NIS is below the gate anyway; a long run well above 1% would indicate a model, noise or timing mismatch.
hints: Run the three steps in order, always predicting first. The dropout step is a prediction with no update, so the covariance keeps growing. NIS is taken from the innovation before its own update.

At step 3 use the state and covariance left by step 2. Predict, then y = z - predicted position and S = predicted P00 + R; NIS = y²/S. Update with the same y and S to get the final state. For the last question, use a chi-square table with 1 degree of freedom to find the probability beyond the gate 6.635.

items.remediation: Common slips on this item: skipping the dropout step entirely (no prediction) gives a final position of 9.098876 m and P00 = 0.30412 m²; forgetting R in S (S = predicted P00) inflates the NIS to 4.342234; reading the gate's coverage (99%) as the exceedance rate confuses coverage with false-alarm rate. Replay with every step predicted, then try a fresh X27 item.
